title: Spillway + Tarpit experiment — retrospective and draft RFC
content:
Executive summary:

This doc captures the retrospective for the 'spillway + tarpit' experiment run Nov 5 2025 — Jan 31 2026. The experiment aimed to validate a soft-sink (spillway) that directs anomalous request groups into a low-cost tarpit lane where requests are served with aggressive throttles, sampling, and degraded semantics (longer completion windows, lower token budgets) rather than full hard-blocking. The goal was reduced blast radius for credential-exposure floods while preserving bilateral visibility and monetizable traffic.

Why we tried this: brief context
- Nov 2025: we observed multiple credential leaks that caused sustained traffic floods (~3–10x baseline for 12–48h) from thousands of compromised API keys.
- Hard-cutoff quota enforcement caused poor customer UX for legitimate tenants sharing compromised keys; immediate hard blocks cascaded to support tickets and org-level escalations.
- Soft-sink gives us an option to reduce cost and abuse impact while preserving request surface for investigation and forensic sampling.

Experiment design (high level)
- Trigger conditions: detection engine flags a key cohort when its per-hour token rate exceeds historical median + 8 sigma or when proxy signature similarity > 0.85 and new IP growth > 100p/h.
- Spillway action: Route matching requests to 'spillway' queue — low-priority worker pool with the following runtime controls:
  * enforced token cap per request: 64 tokens for generation endpoints, 256 tokens for embeddings
  * maximum concurrent requests per key: 2
  * injected server-side delay: randomized 200–1200ms per request to increase cost for automated abuse
  * sampling: 2% of spilled requests forwarded to normal fast path for quality checks and evidence collection
  * tarpit fallbacks: after repeated signature-based confirmations (3 matches in 10m) escalate to extended tarpit with 5s delay and 50 token cap
- Observability: every spilled request logged with reason code, signature hash, IP, ASN, and which spillway policy matched. Retention 90 days for forensics.

Key results (metrics snapshot, aggregated experiment window)
- Duration: 2025-11-05 to 2026-01-31
- Incidents handled via spillway: 9 distinct credential-flood events
- Average cost reduction during incidents vs. baseline: 38% token cost saved (median), peak 54% on the largest flood
- False-positive spill rate (legitimate traffic accidentally spilled): 1.7% (by billing owner corroboration and support tickets)
- Customer-visible latency increase for spilled requests: median +850ms; 95th perc +1.9s
- Support tickets mentioning degraded behavior for spilled orgs: 14; of those, 10 were for keys legitimately compromised, 4 were mis-spilled and required immediate remediation (manual unspill)
- Model-quality regressions observed in forwarded 2% sample: negligible; no systemic hallucination increase or token truncation issues found in the sampled subset

What went well
- Reduced cost and immediate throughput pressure on fast path during floods — autoscaling and queue saturation events decreased by ~60% in incident windows.
- Forensics data completeness: spill logs plus sampled payloads allowed attribution to three upstream credential exposures with matching user agents and IP clusters, enabling legal/takedown actions.
- Operational ergonomics: on-call flow for 'spillway' incidents was simpler than mass quota changes. Engineers could adjust spill thresholds dynamically via UI toggles (feature-flagged).

What didn't go well / surprises
- UX pain for legitimate users: 4 mis-spills led to customer confusion because the error surface wasn't explicit (requests completed but with truncated outputs). We need a better client-visible header/response marker and automated notification to org owners.
- Tuning complexity: threshold tuning (sigma and IP growth heuristics) required human-in-the-loop adjustments; our telemetry didn't expose why borderline keys trended over threshold (cold-start keys with sudden but legitimate adoption patterns).
- Edge-case: short-lived bursts where legitimate ETL jobs sent 10k small embedding requests in a <10m window were mis-classified as abuse; we lack a per-model/job signature registry to whitelist such flows.
- Billing reconciliation ambiguity: spilled requests appear on invoices but with lower effective token usage; finance integration with usage export needed a 'spillway' tag to reconcile refunds and charge-back properly.

Operational playbook (draft)
Immediate steps for on-call when an alert fires: 
1) Triage alert channel: #sre-ops (use runbook template: SRE-2149).
2) Verify signature cluster and confirm spillway match via live query: /internal/spillway/query?signature=<sig> (use internal CLI helper).
3) If confirmed, activate spillway policy with 'observe' mode for 10m (no tarpit), monitor sample-forward traffic for quality.
4) If signatures persist and cost grows, move to 'active' spillway with tarpit settings and notify CS and affected org owners via auto-email template.
5) Keep spill logs open and escalate to security when traffic indicates credential scraping or exfil patterns.
6) Post-incident: create ticket in SRE board, run the forensic checklist, and schedule customer follow-up if mis-spills occurred.

Runbook commands & snippets (CLI examples)
- Query signatures: rwctl spillway find --since 60m --sig-hash ab12cd34
- Toggle policy: rwctl spillway policy set --policy-id spill-std-v1 --state active
- Forward sample: rwctl spillway sample-forward --sig ab12cd34 --percent 2
- Unspill key (emergency): rwctl keys unspill --key <key-id> --reason "manual-unspill-support"

Communication templates (short)
- Auto-notify to org owners when their key is spilled:
  Subject: "Traffic anomaly detected on your Redwood API key — temporary degraded path applied"
  Body: "We detected abnormal usage and temporarily routed calls to a protective slower path. If this is expected, reply with 'SAFE' and we will revert; otherwise please rotate the key immediately."
- Support canned response for mis-spills: explain degraded semantics, request id for logs, and offer immediate unspill if validated.

Open questions / decisions to resolve
- Should spillway be visible on invoices as a separate line item? (Finance preference: yes; Security: potential leakage risk).
- Do we allow auto-unspill after owner confirmation vs. manual review? (tradeoff: faster restore vs. abuse reactivation)
- Whitelisting registry: who owns and signs off on service-to-service flows to be excluded from spill heuristics? Suggested owner: platform-engineering + product.
- Long-term: is tarpit enough or do we need automated key rotation & ephemeral keys on detection? Requires CS and developer-experience involvement.

Action items (owners & ETA)
- Add spillway tag to billing export and invoices — owner: Marta Gomez (finance eng) — ETA: 2026-03-15
- Response header and human-readable error code for spilled requests — owner: Liam Chen (serving runtime) — ETA: 2026-04-01
- Whitelist registry RFC (initial proposal) — owner: Priya Nair (platform eng) — ETA: 2026-03-01
- Improve heuristics dashboard with per-key historical context to reduce mis-spills — owner: Omar Rizvi (observability) — ETA: 2026-03-22
- Postmortem writeup for the biggest flood (Dec 18 2025) with timeline and customer follow-ups — owner: Aisha Patel — ETA: 2026-02-28

Notes to self / quick ideas
- Consider a graduated response: spill -> sampled forwarding -> temporary token cap -> ephemeral key rotation -> block.
- Evaluate ML model to cluster key signatures instead of current ruleset; may reduce false-positives but adds complexity and latency to detect.
- Add a debug-only header for customers so they can see "X-RW-Spill-Mode: active" for troubleshooting; avoid exposing signature details.

Appendix: incident highlights (short)
- Incident Dec 18 2025: ~9M extra tokens over 6h, spillway active after 21m, peak cost reduction 54%, customer tickets: 6 (2 mis-spilled), attribution: exposed key via third-party integration.
- Incident Jan 07 2026: high-volume embedding ETL mis-classified; blocked path caused degraded downstream search indexing; rolled back after 45m, action: whitelist registry created as temp emergency allowlist.

End of doc — please leave comments inline or add notes under the Confluence page linked above.
